children.text: A Safety Net, Not Comprehensive Insurance

A common misconception is that Medicare pays for everything once you turn 65. It does not. Traditional Medicare was designed in 1965 as a safety net against catastrophic costs, not as a comprehensive benefit, and it still carries substantial cost-sharing and significant coverage exclusions. Understanding these gaps is the single best way to understand why the Medigap and Medicare Advantage markets exist.

Cost-sharing in traditional Medicare comes in three forms: deductibles you pay before coverage kicks in, coinsurance (a share of each cost), and premiums for ongoing coverage. The dollar figures change every year; the structure does not.

The most consequential design feature is what traditional Medicare lacks: an out-of-pocket maximum. Unlike employer plans and Medicare Advantage, Original Medicare Parts A and B set no annual cap on what a beneficiary can owe — a single catastrophic illness can generate unlimited 20 percent coinsurance.

Original Medicare (Parts A + B) has no annual out-of-pocket maximum. This is the central financial risk of traditional Medicare and the main reason most beneficiaries add Medigap or choose Medicare Advantage.
Part A Cost-Sharing (Hospital)

Part A cost-sharing is organized around the "benefit period," a concept that surprises many beneficiaries. A benefit period begins when you are admitted as an inpatient and ends only after you have been out of a hospital or skilled nursing facility for 60 consecutive days. The deductible is charged per benefit period, not per year — so two separate hospitalizations months apart can each trigger the full deductible.

In 2025, the inpatient hospital deductible is $1,676 per benefit period. Days 1–60 carry no additional coinsurance after the deductible. Days 61–90 cost $419 per day. Beyond 90 days, you tap into 60 "lifetime reserve days" at $838 per day — and once used, those reserve days are gone forever.

Skilled nursing facility (SNF) coverage follows a separate schedule and has a critical precondition: Medicare only pays for SNF care after a qualifying inpatient hospital stay of at least three days. SNF days 1–20 carry no coinsurance; days 21–100 cost $209.50 per day in 2025; and after day 100, the beneficiary pays the full cost.

body.message: Medicare only covers SNF care after a 3-day inpatient hospital stay. Time spent under "observation status" — even overnight — does not count as inpatient, so patients who think they were admitted can be denied SNF coverage. This is a frequent and costly trap.
body.title: The 3-day rule and "observation status"

children.text: Part B Cost-Sharing (Medical)

Part B covers physician visits, outpatient care, preventive services, and durable medical equipment. In 2025, the standard Part B premium is $185.00 per month and the annual deductible is $257. After the deductible, beneficiaries typically pay 20 percent coinsurance of the Medicare-approved amount for most services.

That 20 percent has no ceiling. For a routine office visit it is trivial; for an expensive course of chemotherapy, dialysis, or specialty infusions billed under Part B, the 20 percent share can run into the tens of thousands of dollars in a single year — with no out-of-pocket maximum to stop it.

Higher-income beneficiaries pay more than the standard premium through IRMAA, the Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount, which adds surcharges to both Part B and Part D premiums above set income thresholds.

children.text: What Medicare Does NOT Cover

Beyond cost-sharing, traditional Medicare simply excludes whole categories of care that older adults frequently need. Routine dental, vision, and hearing care — including most dentures, eyeglasses, and hearing aids — are not covered by Original Medicare.

The largest gap is long-term care. Medicare does not pay for custodial long-term care — help with bathing, dressing, eating, and other daily activities in a nursing home or at home over the long run. Medicare covers only short-term, skilled care for recovery. Long-term custodial care is paid out of pocket, by long-term care insurance, or by Medicaid once a person spends down their assets.

These exclusions are not minor. They are precisely the benefits that Medicare Advantage plans advertise — many MA plans add dental, vision, and hearing benefits — and they are a major reason beneficiaries weigh MA against Original Medicare plus a supplement.

children.text: How Medigap Fills the Gaps

Because Original Medicare has no out-of-pocket maximum and substantial cost-sharing, most traditional-Medicare beneficiaries buy a Medicare Supplement policy, known as Medigap. Sold by private insurers, Medigap plans are standardized into lettered plans (such as Plan G and Plan N) so that the same letter offers the same benefits no matter which company sells it.

Medigap covers cost-sharing in Original Medicare — Part A and Part B coinsurance and copayments, and depending on the plan, deductibles. By capping the beneficiary’s exposure, Medigap effectively creates the out-of-pocket protection that Original Medicare itself lacks.

But Medigap does not fill the benefit gaps. Medigap plans generally do not cover dental, vision, hearing, or long-term care. For those, beneficiaries must buy separate standalone policies — or choose a Medicare Advantage plan that bundles such benefits in. This trade-off, cost protection versus added benefits, is the core choice every new beneficiary faces.

body.content: Consider a Part B patient on an expensive specialty infusion drug billed at $300,000 a year. Under Original Medicare alone, the 20% coinsurance — about $60,000 — would fall on the patient with no cap to stop it. A Medigap Plan G would cover that Part B coinsurance after the small Part B deductible, turning a potentially ruinous bill into a predictable, modest cost. This is exactly the financial risk Medigap was built to address.
body.title: The Catastrophic-Cost Scenario

On $400,000 of services that 20% share runs into the tens of thousands with nothing to cap it — which is why most beneficiaries add Medigap or choose Medicare Advantage (which is required to have an out-of-pocket cap).
